papers.title: Parkinson's disease burden, inequality, and projections in Asia, 1990-2050.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a growing neurological and public health challenge in Asia, but evidence integrating long-term trends, socioeconomic inequality, demographic drivers, and future burden remains limited. METHODS: We analysed Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 estimates of PD incidence, prevalence, and disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) in 51 Asian countries and territories from 1990 to 2023. We assessed age-standardised rates, temporal trends, Socio-demographic Index-related inequality, demographic decomposition, frontier gaps, age-defined early- and late-onset PD, and sex-specific projections to 2050. RESULTS: In 2023, Asia had an estimated 751,892 incident cases, 6,383,013 prevalent cases, and 4,363,170 DALYs. Age-standardised incidence, prevalence, and DALY rates were 13.97, 119.93, and 83.90 per 100,000 population, respectively. From 1990 to 2023, incidence and prevalence rates increased (estimated annual percentage changes, 0.98% and 1.41%), whereas the DALY rate increased modestly (0.12%). West Asia had the highest age-standardised burden. Inequality widened for incidence and prevalence, while DALY burden shifted towards lower-SDI settings. Changes in population age structure made the largest contribution to the increase in absolute burden. By 2050, PD burden is projected to reach 1.94 million incident cases, 17.74 million prevalent cases, and 16.01 million DALYs. CONCLUSIONS: The rapidly increasing and unequal PD burden in Asia requires ageing- and development-sensitive strategies for surveillance, diagnosis, treatment, rehabilitation, long-term care, caregiver support, and environmental risk reduction.

papers.title: Early caudate involvement marks a Lewy body spectrum phenotype in parkinsonism: a 5-year longitudinal study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinsonian syndromes are increasingly recognized as part of a heterogeneous spectrum of Lewy body diseases, ranging from Parkinson's disease (PD) to dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB). Identifying early markers of clinical heterogeneity remains challenging. OBJECTIVE: To investigate whether striatal dopaminergic denervation patterns on DAT-SPECT are associated with distinct clinical phenotypes and long-term cognitive trajectories in early parkinsonism. METHODS: Twenty-eight patients with early parkinsonism fulfilling clinical diagnostic criteria for PD underwent DAT-SPECT and were classified according to the topography of dopaminergic denervation into isolated putaminal involvement (P group) or combined putaminal and caudate involvement (PC group). Motor, neuropsychiatric, and cognitive assessments, including the MoCA, were performed at baseline and after 5 years. RESULTS: At baseline, patients with caudate involvement (n CONCLUSION: Early caudate dopaminergic denervation identifies a parkinsonian phenotype associated with greater motor severity, neuropsychiatric manifestations, and accelerated cognitive decline. Its longitudinal evolution may reflect a trajectory toward the cognitive and neuropsychiatric end of the Lewy body disease spectrum, including a DLB-like phenotype. DAT-SPECT may provide prognostic information beyond its diagnostic utility.

papers.title: The metabolic-brain axis: GLP-1 signaling, insulin resistance, and obesity pharmacotherapy in neurodegeneration.
papers.abstract: The intersection of metabolic disease and neurodegeneration represents one of the most consequential frontiers in translational neuroscience. Converging epidemiological, mechanistic, and pharmacological evidence supports a bidirectional metabolic-brain axis in which systemic insulin resistance, obesity, and chronic metabolic inflammation are associated with and may contribute to alterations in neuronal survival, synaptic plasticity, and neuroimmune homeostasis. GLP-1 receptor agonists, originally developed for glycemic control and weight management, have therefore been investigated as potential disease-modifying therapies across Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and related neurodegenerative conditions through mechanisms including neuronal PKA activation, microglial NLRP3 suppression, mitochondrial biogenesis, and restoration of AQP4 perivascular localization that may contribute to glymphatic waste clearance. Direct human evidence for these CNS mechanisms remains limited or absent, with current support derived primarily from preclinical models and indirect human data, as detailed in Table 1, warranting dedicated investigation in the context of GLP-1 receptor agonism. papers.title: Targeting lipid peroxidation-derived aldehydes in Parkinson's Disease and ageing: Antioxidant investigations and mechanistic insights.
papers.abstract: Oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation are increasingly recognized as age-related drivers of neurodegeneration, with Parkinson's disease (PD) representing a condition of heightened vulnerability. Among lipid peroxidation products, reactive aldehydes including 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal, malondialdehyde, acrolein, 4-hydroxy-2-hexenal, and crotonaldehyde have emerged not only as biomarkers of oxidative damage, but also as active mediators of neuronal dysfunction. Owing to their electrophilic nature, these aldehydes interact with nucleophilic residues, including cysteine, lysine, and histidine, forming covalent adducts that impair proteostasis, mitochondrial function, and redox signaling. Under physiological conditions, lipid peroxidation-derived aldehydes (LPDAs) are detoxified through glutathione-dependent conjugation and oxidoreductase-mediated metabolism. However, ageing progressively impairs these protective systems, promoting aldehyde accumulation and increasing dopaminergic vulnerability. We propose that PD may reflect, at least in part, an age-dependent impairment of aldehyde detoxification in addition to increased reactive oxygen species production. Although current experimental and clinical evidence supports the pathogenic relevance of some LPDAs in PD, antioxidant-based interventions have yielded inconsistent clinical outcomes. Within this framework, antioxidant strategies can be interpreted according to their functional impact on aldehyde burden. Approaches aimed at restoring glutathione homeostasis or activating Nrf2-dependent pathways may enhance endogenous detoxification systems and thereby support aldehyde clearance. More directly targeted approaches include strategies that enhance aldehyde metabolism, such as pharmacological activation of ALDH2. Overall, shifting the therapeutic focus from radical scavenging to the modulation of aldehyde burden through combined upstream and downstream interventions represents a promising but still underexplored avenue in PD

papers.title: High-altitude environments elevate central and peripheral α-synuclein levels and accelerate PD-related pathology.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: High-altitude exposure has been linked to an increased risk of Parkinson's disease (PD), potentially through hypoxic neuronal damage, yet the involvement of α-synuclein (α-syn) remains poorly understood. This study integrates population-based surveys, animal experiments, and clinical cross-sectional data to elucidate the role of high-altitude environments in PD pathogenesis. METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted among middle-aged and elderly high-altitude residents. Additional cohorts (low-altitude PD patients, low-altitude controls, and high-altitude controls) were enrolled for plasma and erythrocytic α-syn measurement, and a subset of PD patients underwent transcranial sonography to assess correlations between erythrocyte indices and substantia nigra echogenicity. A53T transgenic mice were exposed to high altitude for six months and evaluated by behavioral tests, omics sequencing, α-syn assays, and immunohistochemistry. Erythrocyte-derived extracellular vesicles from PD patients were intravenously injected into wild-type mice to assess brain entry. RESULTS: The crude prevalence of PD tended to be higher in high-altitude populations than the national average. A53T mice exposed to high altitude displayed more severe motor deficits, elevated brain α-syn levels, and pronounced dopaminergic neuron loss. Omics analyses revealed enrichment of pathways related to IL-17, sphingosine-1-phosphate signaling, and oxidative stress in brain tissue from high-altitude versus low-altitude A53T mice, suggesting blood-brain barrier disruption and impaired α-syn clearance. In peripheral blood, both high-altitude mice and humans exhibited elevated α-syn levels compared with their low-altitude counterparts, and erythrocyte indices correlated positively with α-syn levels. papers.title: Metabolic endotyping for mechanism-informed Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease trials.
papers.abstract: Metabolically targeted therapies for Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease have yielded mixed results despite convergent evidence implicating three interconnected axes of metabolic dysfunction: insulin signaling, cellular bioenergetics, and lipid-lysosomal biology. We argue that this pattern partly reflects a trial-design problem: therapeutics such as glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists, terazosin, and stearoyl-CoA desaturase inhibitors generally have been tested in biologically unselected populations, with endpoints often distal to the targeted mechanism. We propose as a testable hypothesis that a metabolic endotype-a measurable, biomarker-supported pattern of metabolic dysfunction-spans subsets of both diseases and that failure to enrich for this endotype could dilute therapeutic signals in all-comer trials. We outline a modular four-tier framework integrating prodromal risk, metabolic vulnerability, pathway-specific confirmation, and mechanistic deep phenotyping to make Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease trials more interpretable and therapeutically informative.

papers.title: From dosage alteration to amplification strategies: mechanistically defined alpha-synuclein mouse models for Parkinson's disease therapy development.
papers.abstract: A major challenge for identifying a disease-modifying cure for Parkinson's disease (PD) is creating models resembling key features of the disease including resting tremor, bradykinesia, muscle rigidity and gait disturbances. In addition, PD patients often develop cognitive symptoms that are associated with pathology in neocortical areas. Initially, PD rodent models were generated primarily by chemical neurotoxins that induce an acute loss of dopaminergic neurons. Upon discovery of familial-PD-linked genetic mutations in the SNCA gene-encoding α-synuclein (αS)-mice carrying these mutations provided deeper insight into the pathologic role of this synaptic protein throughout the brain. αS transgenic mouse models stand out for their ability to develop intraneuronal lesions that are rich in αS phospho-serine 129, a histopathological signature of the human PD brain. Recent advances in αS protein biochemistry led to the generation of mice carrying strategic amplifications of familial-PD-linked αS mutants, resulting in more pronounced neurodegeneration and progressive phenotype development. Here we review advances of αS transgenic mouse model development with a focus on strategic mutations that may have greater potential for identifying underlying disease mechanisms than classical single-mutant and wild-type αS overexpressing mice. We also present how the mice are currently used in testing drug efficacy and target engagement for PD drug discovery and outline strategies for utilizing such mice in basic and translational research.

papers.title: Integrative Evolutionary and Structural Analysis of GBA1 Provides Insights Into Mutation-Specific Effects Associated With Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: GBA1 encodes lysosomal acid β-glucosidase (glucocerebrosidase [GCase]), a key lysosomal enzyme and one of the most important genetic factors in Parkinson's disease (PD). Yet how different GBA1 variants influence PD-related molecular pathology remains incompletely understood. Here, we integrated phylogenetic, comparative sequence, structural, docking, and molecular dynamics analyses to identify evolutionarily constrained features of GBA1 that may influence its interaction with α-synuclein (SNCA) and thereby contribute to PD pathogenesis. Phylogenetic reconstruction indicated that GBA1 originated early in bilaterian evolution and was maintained as a single-copy gene in the sampled taxa, consistent with strong functional constraint. Sequence-based analyses across sarcopterygian lineages further supported pervasive purifying selection, especially within the TIM barrel catalytic domain. Comparative structural analyses highlighted a conformationally sensitive segment spanning Residues 379-389, which includes catalytic and neighboring residues and showed recurrent involvement in both mammalian evolution and PD-associated mutant proteins. Docking and molecular dynamics simulations of wild-type and mutant GBA1-SNCA complexes indicated that PD-associated substitutions can remodel hydrogen-bond networks and influence the conformational landscape of the GBA1-SNCA complex in a mutation-specific manner. Although no statistically significant differences in global structural or energetic properties were detected, individual variants exhibited distinct patterns of conformational deviation, flexibility, and interaction dynamics relative to wild type. In particular, Residues 387-389 emerged as part of a structurally responsive region linked to altered GBA1-SNCA association. Together, these findings highlight candidate structural determinants for future experimental studies of GBA1-associated neurodegeneration.

papers.title: The pathological roles of intrinsically disordered proteins in lysosomal acidification dysfunction in neurodegenerative diseases.

papers.title: Acceptability of Wearable Digital Devices for Remote Continuous Mobility Monitoring in People With Parkinson Disease and Carers: Qualitative Study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson disease (PD) impairs mobility and motor function, making accurate mobility assessment important for effective management and treatment planning. Traditional clinical assessments often rely on periodic clinical evaluations, which may not capture day-to-day symptom fluctuations. Wearable devices offer a promising alternative with continuous, objective tracking of mobility (eg, gait). However, although these tools provide valuable insights for patients and clinicians, their successful implementation depends on their acceptability to users. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to explore the acceptability of wearable devices for remote continuous mobility monitoring in PD from the perspectives of people with PD and informal carers. METHODS: This international qualitative study used purposive sampling to recruit a diverse sample of 72 people with PD and 20 informal carers from the United Kingdom, Ireland, Belgium, Germany, Spain, and the United States. Participants were recruited between June 2023 and February 2026 through multiple community-based routes. One-to-one semistructured interviews, conducted online, via telephone, or in person, explored views on wearable devices for digital mobility assessment. Interview data were analyzed using Braun and Clarke's 6-phase reflexive thematic analysis. RESULTS: Most people with PD were generally open to wearable monitoring when it could capture motor fluctuations between "on" and "off" periods that were difficult to convey during clinical appointments, reduce reliance on memory, provide objective evidence to support treatment and medication discussions and self-advocacy, and track changes in mobility over time, which some felt could be reassuring. Acceptability depended on devices having a clear purpose, requiring minimal effort, and being easy to use. papers.title: Prevalence of many comorbidities is similar irrespective of the time since HIV diagnosis in persons ageing with HIV who have survived to age 65 years.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To compare the prevalence of comorbidity in persons with HIV ≥65 years of age based on the time from HIV diagnosis. DESIGN: Cross-sectional observational cohort study. METHODS: Data was collected from 540 participants in the CHANGE HIV (Correlates of Healthy Aging in Geriatric HIV) study, a longitudinal study of HIV in persons aged 65 years and older from seven primary and tertiary care centres in Canada between 2019 and 2026. We compared the baseline prevalence of comorbidities stratified by the cumulative time since known HIV diagnosis (<20 years, 20-30 years and >30 years) and controlled for demographic, HIV and lifestyle factors. RESULTS: The cohort was 90% male, median age 69 years, 76% white, median CD4 561 cells/mm3 CONCLUSIONS: Prevalence of many comorbidities was not increased in those with longer time since HIV diagnosis. Lifestyle factors (smoking, substance use and diet) are important contributors to non-infectious comorbidities in this population, and increased prevalence of cancer reinforces the importance of preventative screening.
